units: two joinery workshops stand on the same street
the first workshop shapes wood by hand with plain tools
the second workshop uses machines and employs three workers
the workers in the second workshop mostly watch screens
the hand workshop makes little but sells at a high price
the mechanised workshop makes a great deal and sells cheaply
the hand workshop depends on its reputation to survive
the mechanised workshop depends on the flow of orders
the two owners greet each other in the evening
text: Two joinery workshops stand at either end of the same shopping street. In the first, a seasoned cabinetmaker cuts the wood by hand. His tools are plain, his movements unhurried, and every piece leaves his palms after a long run of trial and error. In the second, machines slice identical boards, and three workers spend far more time watching screens than touching timber. The hand workshop shifts few pieces, yet each one goes for a high price, since the buyer pays for patience as much as for wood. The mechanised workshop shifts a great deal, cheaply, and leans on volume to cover heavier costs. The first lives as long as the reputation of the hand lasts; the second holds while the orders keep coming. In the evening the two owners nod to each other, aware that they sell the same thing by opposite routes.

units: the writer names three weaknesses in stock management
the first weakness concerns demand forecasting
forecasts rest on old records that are never corrected
warehouses fill up with items nobody buys
the second weakness concerns the costing of stock
a surplus of goods locks up cash that is needed elsewhere
the third weakness concerns the behaviour of buyers
managers order too much for fear of running short
the writer holds that correcting the forecast alone is not enough
text: Three weaknesses eat away at stock management among mid-sized manufacturers, and they deserve to be named plainly. The first sits in forecasting. Demand is projected from old records, with no correction for past breaks in supply, so warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys. The second sits in costing. A surplus batch locks up cash that will be missed elsewhere, and a crammed storeroom soon grows expensive to keep. The third sits in behaviour. Purchasing managers would rather order generously than face an empty shelf, an understandable reflex and a ruinous one. A loss-making year seldom grows out of one isolated mistake. It grows out of three habits that feed each other. Tightening the forecast while leaving untouched whatever rewards the buyers will bring nothing better than temporary relief.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs a weaving cooperative
she started as an apprentice at a hand loom
her first job was to mend broken threads
the experienced weavers were glad to hand that job over
she was later moved to the receiving of raw materials
that post taught her about prices and delivery times
she trained in accounting away from the workshop
she proposed selling without going through a middleman
takings rose and the workshop took on more staff
text: The woman who now runs a weaving cooperative began her working life behind a hand loom, as an apprentice. Her first job was to tie up broken threads, a slow and thankless chore the experienced weavers were glad to hand over. After two seasons she was moved to goods inward, where the raw materials arrived, and there she learnt about prices, delivery times and margins. She then left the workshop to train in accounting, and came back with a precise proposal: supply the retailers directly, instead of going through a middleman who took his share along the way. The cooperative hesitated, then agreed to a limited trial. Takings rose, and two more spinners were taken on. Today she runs the house she knew as a child, and hands the delicate orders to the apprentices, as was once done for her.

units: a training scheme for jobseekers is assessed
the scheme is held to be useful but badly calibrated
the modules teach skills that are too narrow
employers want candidates who can move from one post to another
trainees find work but leave it quickly
the assessor puts those departures down to the narrowness of the training
spells inside a firm produce better outcomes
the assessor recommends longer spells inside a firm
text: The training scheme under review does genuine good, though the way it has been calibrated is open to question. Its modules teach narrow skills, cut to fit a single task, while employers are asking for candidates who can move from one post to another as the order book changes. The mismatch between the two shows up in an effect that can be measured. Trainees land a job quickly enough, then leave before the probation period is out, unable to cope with the side duties handed to them. Spells spent inside a firm produce far sturdier outcomes, most likely because the trainee watches the whole chain rather than one isolated link. The assessment therefore argues for longer spells of that kind, even at the cost of trimming the theory, which looks redundant beside the manuals handed out at the start.

units: the writer tells a friend about his soap business
making the soap by hand takes up all his evenings
the profits were too thin at the outset
the cost of sending parcels swallowed the margin
the writer has cut his catalogue back to three scents
he now leaves his crates at a shared depot instead of posting each parcel
the business has paid its way since those changes
the writer asks his friend to come and see the workshop
text: I owe you news of the soap business, and this letter of mine is a good deal later than it should be. You remember what I used to moan about: making the stuff by hand swallowed every evening of mine, and the profit stayed thin. Well, I have finally put my finger on the culprit. It was the sending out. Each parcel went off on its own, with its wrapping and its docket, and the margin melted away before it ever reached the buyer. So I made up my mind. I cut the catalogue back to three scents, the ones that always sold, and stopped chasing one-off orders. My crates now go to a shared depot, and the shopkeepers come and take what they want. Since then the business pays, and I sleep. Come and see the workshop when you are passing; you will judge the difference, and you will leave loaded.

units: an economist answers questions on the funding of new businesses
she compares a bank loan with letting an investor take a stake
a loan must be repaid even when trade falls away
a loan leaves the founder in command of his own choices
an investor asks for nothing if the venture fails
an investor wants a share of the decisions and of the profits to come
she advises borrowing for a trade with steady takings
she advises taking a partner for uncertain and costly projects
text: An economist who studies how young businesses are funded has agreed to sit down and take our questions. Borrow, or bring in a shareholder? She refuses to settle the matter in a single word, and lays out the comparison. A loan, she explains, sets a repayment date that falls due even when sales sag; against that, it leaves the founder in full command of his own choices. A partner taking a stake asks for nothing if the venture fails, but he buys a share of the decisions to come and of the profits to come. So which does she recommend? A trade with steady takings carries a fixed repayment easily and does well to borrow. An uncertain project, dear to set up and slow to pay off, will seldom survive without a partner willing to wait. It comes down, she says, to how regular the money coming in is.

units: two market traders talk once the covered market has shut
the fruit seller lists her difficulties
she mentions the rent on her pitch
she mentions the crates of damaged goods
she mentions her supplier arriving late
the cheese seller answers that her own troubles are different
the cheese seller mentions the cold she has to hold steady
the cheese seller mentions her customers growing fewer
the two traders agree to share a van
text: The shutters of the covered market had only just come down when the fruit seller began the long list of her troubles. She spoke of the rent on her pitch, which climbed every season while the aisle stayed as shabby as ever. She spoke of the battered crates, of the bruised peaches no buyer would take and she herself would carry home at dusk. She spoke last of her supplier, whose van pulled up after opening, once the shoppers had already come and gone. The cheese seller listened, then said her own troubles went by other names: the cold, hard to hold steady all day long, the electricity bill that follows it, and the queue at her counter thinning week by week. For a while neither of them said anything. Then they agreed to hire a van between them and fetch their crates together before dawn.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text traces the coming of trade associations
the early craftsmen worked scattered and without shared rules
neighbouring workshops first agreed on identical measures
the next agreement covered the length of apprenticeship
the associations then set floor prices
floor prices sheltered members from competition on rates
the associations also decided who might open a workshop
that closing of the door ended up holding back new methods
the associations lost their power as manufactories grew
text: Before any organisation existed, craftsmen in the same trade worked each on his own, with no shared measure and no common rule. The first agreement between neighbouring workshops concerned size: a plank, a pot, a length of cloth had to answer to one template, or else the buyer had no way of comparing. Next came apprenticeship, whose length and stages were laid down. Trade associations, flourishing by then, extended their grip to rates as well, imposing a floor price that sheltered their members from ruinous undercutting. Finally they kept for themselves the right to allow a workshop to open, and that closing of the door, protective at the outset, discouraged fresh methods. Once manufactories gathered hundreds of hands under one roof, the associations lost their authority.

units: the text explains why a farm product grows dearer after a poor harvest
a poor harvest cuts the quantity to be had
the buyers stay as numerous as before
scarcity pushes up the price paid to the grower
the firms that process the crop pass the rise on to their own rates
some buyers turn instead to a substitute product
the heavier demand pushes up the price of the substitute as well
prices come down again when the next harvest is plentiful
text: A poor harvest does a good deal more than empty the granaries: it sets off a chain of effects that runs all the way to the market stall. The quantity to be had falls while the buyers stay as numerous as before, so each of them agrees to pay more to secure his own share, and the price handed to the grower climbs. Firms that process the crop watch their own bills swell in the same way, and pass the weight on to the rates they charge. Part of the custom then gives up and turns to a neighbouring foodstuff. That shift has a consequence few people expect: the substitute, suddenly in heavy demand, grows dearer in its turn, even though its own harvest was an ordinary one. Balance comes back only with a generous season, when the granaries fill again and the pressure on prices slackens.

units: a bakery in a small town threw away part of its baking every evening
the baker baked the same quantity without regard to what sold
the waste threatened to unbalance the accounts of the shop
the apprentice wrote down the unsold loaves over several weeks
the record showed that the waste piled up at the end of the week
the batch at the end of the week was cut back
the loaves left on the shelves are sold cheaply before closing
the waste has fallen sharply
a neighbouring shop copied the method
text: Every evening the baker of a small valley town filled a sack with the loaves nobody had taken, and the sack went off to the farm nearby. He had baked the same quantity since the day he opened, without a glance at what actually sold, and the waste was gnawing at an already thin margin. The apprentice suggested counting. Over several weeks she wrote down in an exercise book how many loaves came back, what shape they were, which flour had gone into them. The record left no room for doubt: the waste piled up at the end of the week, when families baked for themselves. So the last batch of the week was cut by a third, and whatever still sat on the shelves half an hour before closing went at a knock-down price. The waste shrank, the till breathed, and the butcher across the road, who had watched it all, began keeping the same book.
